strengths: The paper tackles a relevant low-level vision problem and makes a coherent case that moire artifacts can be usefully decomposed into high-frequency texture corruption and low-frequency color distortion. The dual-branch design, with crop training for high frequencies and resize training for low frequencies, is well motivated and fits the empirical behavior shown in the paper.

Reported results are strong on two high-resolution demoireing benchmarks. Freqformer improves over prior demoireing methods on FHDMi across PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS, and is competitive or best on UHDM while using only 6.065M parameters.

The experimental section includes meaningful ablations for the low-frequency resize strategy, learnable versus fixed FCT, dual-branch training, branch-level performance, and hierarchical fusion/RDDB components. These ablations support the main design choices better than many incremental restoration papers.

The model-efficiency argument is plausible: the method is substantially smaller than several compared restoration models and has reported 4K FLOPs close to efficient demoireing baselines while achieving better quality metrics.

The paper is generally clear about the pipeline and training procedure, with useful visualizations of decomposed images and qualitative comparisons illustrating residual moire and color errors in baselines.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than high. The frequency decomposition is a simple fixed low-pass/high-pass recursive filter inspired by prior work, while the attention block combines familiar ingredients such as RDDBs, channel attention, depth-wise convolutions, gated FFNs, and transformer-style restoration blocks. The contribution is mainly an effective integration for demoireing.

Several reproducibility details are missing or underspecified, including the decomposition level L, channel widths, exact crop/resize handling at inference, training time, and complete code availability. The abstract states that code is publicly available, but the URL is blank in the manuscript.

The evaluation is limited to two datasets and does not test cross-dataset generalization, robustness to unseen display/camera conditions, or real user-captured images outside the benchmark distributions. This matters because the paper claims suitability for practical high-resolution deployment.

The deployment claims are stronger than the evidence. The paper reports parameters and FLOPs, but not runtime, memory usage, tiling behavior, or quality/speed on actual edge devices; all implementation details mention an RTX 4090.

Some important contemporary baselines discussed in related work, such as P-BiC and recent raw/sRGB demoireing methods where applicable, are not included in the main quantitative comparison. This makes the state-of-the-art claim somewhat less conclusive.

The ablation against Haar wavelets reports catastrophic performance but gives little diagnostic detail; this comparison may be sensitive to implementation or fusion choices and is not fully convincing as evidence that Haar-based approaches are intrinsically unsuitable.

Writing and presentation contain minor issues, including informal phrasing, typos, and some awkward mathematical notation. These do not undermine the core contribution but should be polished for publication.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant low-level vision problem: high-resolution RGB image demoiréing, where separating texture-like artifacts from color distortions is a plausible modeling direction.
The proposed system is compact relative to several baselines and reports competitive or best results on FHDMi and UHDM for SSIM/LPIPS, with a reasonable parameter count and reported 4K FLOP cost.
The ablations attempt to isolate several design choices, including crop versus resize training, learnable frequency composition, hierarchical fusion, and RDDB usage.
weaknesses: The claimed novelty is weak. The frequency decomposition is essentially a fixed Gaussian/Laplacian-pyramid-style filtering process adapted from prior restoration work, and the transformer/channel-attention blocks are close to established restoration architectures such as Restormer-style channel attention with depthwise convolutions. The paper repeatedly presents these as novel without clearly separating borrowed components from new contributions.

The experimental evidence is not convincing enough for the strength of the claims. The paper omits important recent demoiréing comparisons despite citing them, especially P-BiC, and mostly compares against older methods or general restoration models. This makes the state-of-the-art claim fragile.

Reproducibility is poor. The abstract says the code is publicly available but the URL is blank. Important details are missing or unclear, including the decomposition level L, exact crop/resize inference handling, training cost, checkpoint selection, baseline retraining protocols, and whether reported baseline numbers are reproduced under identical settings.

Several ablations are hard to interpret. Tables 3 and 5 report very high PSNR values for low/high branches that are not directly comparable to full-image demoiréing, but the paper does not clearly explain the evaluation targets or implications. The Haar comparison is especially unconvincing: reporting PSNR 13.32 for a Haar variant suggests an implementation or adaptation failure rather than a fair comparison to wavelet-based methods.

The paper overclaims deployment suitability. It mentions edge devices and efficient 4K inference, but provides no actual latency, memory, device-side measurements, or comparison under practical deployment constraints.

The method description and writing quality are below ECCV standard in places, with imprecise phrasing, formatting artifacts in figures/equations, and casual language such as 'awesome benefits.' More importantly, the conceptual justification for why the low-frequency branch should correct dataset color shifts is asserted rather than rigorously validated.

The evaluation is narrow: only paired benchmark metrics are used, with no robustness tests across displays/cameras, no cross-dataset generalization, no perceptual/user study despite emphasizing visual quality, and no analysis of failure cases or limitations. For a demoiréing paper, these omissions materially weaken the scientific case.

strengths: The paper addresses a concrete and practically important low-level vision problem: high-resolution image demoireing, where both structured texture artifacts and color distortions matter. The motivation for treating these components differently is convincing and well aligned with the observed properties of moire corruption.

The proposed Freqformer framework is technically coherent. The frequency decomposition, dual high-/low-frequency branches, crop-versus-resize training strategy, learnable frequency composition transform, and SA-CA blocks form a consistent design rather than a collection of disconnected tricks.

The empirical results are strong. On FHDMi, the method improves over prior demoireing baselines across PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS, and on UHDM it achieves the best SSIM/LPIPS while remaining competitive in PSNR. The parameter count is also attractive, especially compared with larger demoireing and general restoration models.

The ablation studies support the main design choices: resize training for the low-frequency branch, two-branch frequency training, learnable FCT, and branch-level efficiency are all evaluated. The comparison to both demoireing-specific methods and recent general image restoration models strengthens the experimental case.

The paper is generally clear and easy to follow, with helpful visualizations of the decomposed frequency components and qualitative comparisons that illustrate the claimed improvements in residual moire removal and color recovery.
weaknesses: The novelty is positive but somewhat incremental. Several ingredients are adapted from known image-restoration practice, including blur-based frequency decomposition, encoder-decoder restoration backbones, transformer/channel attention blocks, perceptual loss, and deep supervision. The paper would benefit from sharper articulation of what is fundamentally new beyond this particular combination for demoireing.

The evaluation is limited to supervised in-domain benchmarks. Since real moire artifacts vary significantly across screens, cameras, ISP pipelines, and capture conditions, cross-dataset generalization or evaluation on additional real-world captures would be important to establish robustness beyond FHDMi and UHDM.

The comparison to Haar wavelet decomposition is underdeveloped. Reporting extremely poor Haar-transform results suggests either a mismatch in implementation/training protocol or an unusually unfavorable setup; more careful comparison against wavelet-based alternatives would make the frequency-decomposition claim more convincing.

Some experimental details are not fully sufficient for reproducibility and fair comparison. The manuscript should more explicitly specify code/data release status, exact training schedules for baselines, inference tiling/full-resolution handling, random seeds, evaluator settings, and whether all competing methods were retrained under comparable conditions.

Efficiency claims are promising but incomplete. The paper reports parameters and some FLOPs/speed numbers, but a clearer wall-clock inference comparison, memory usage at 4K, and deployment constraints would better support claims about edge-device suitability.

The writing contains minor polish issues and a few overstatements, such as informal phrasing, occasional typos, and broad claims about disentangling moire patterns that are only indirectly supported by benchmark metrics. These do not undermine the main contribution but should be cleaned up.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and difficult low-level vision problem, especially high-resolution image demoiréing where both texture artifacts and color shifts matter.

The proposed frequency split is simple and well motivated for the task: high-frequency residuals are handled locally while low-frequency color distortion is processed at reduced scale, which is a plausible design for UHD demoiréing.

Experimental results are strong across TIP2018, LCDMoire, FHDMi, and UHDM. Freqformer is best or near-best on the main metrics, with particularly good SSIM/LPIPS on UHDM and clear gains over several demoiréing and general restoration baselines.
The model has a favorable parameter/performance tradeoff: roughly 6M parameters while matching or exceeding larger baselines such as ESDNet-L, MBCNN, MopNet, AdaIR, and MoCE-IR.

The ablation section is useful. It separately studies the proposed transform versus Haar/DCT variants, resize-based low-frequency training, learnable FCT, frequency decomposition, hierarchical fusion, and architectural blocks.
The paper is generally understandable and includes qualitative comparisons that support the quantitative trends.
weaknesses: Originality is moderate rather than high. The decomposition is essentially a smooth low-pass / residual high-pass construction inspired by prior work, and many architectural ingredients, including RDDBs, channel attention, gated FFNs, U-Net-like encoder-decoders, and two-stage training, are familiar. The paper’s novelty lies more in task-specific integration than in a fundamentally new algorithmic principle.

Some claims about DWT/DCT being fundamentally ill-suited, causing error accumulation, spatial discontinuity, or architectural incompatibility are asserted more strongly than they are proven. The ablation compares full model variants with different parameter counts and implementation choices, so it does not fully isolate the transform itself.

The experimental protocol for external baselines is not always sufficiently detailed. Some methods are retrained/adapted, others appear taken from prior results, and fairness depends heavily on training resolution, augmentation, losses, and inference strategy. More exact reproduction details would be needed for high confidence.

The code availability line is incomplete, and important reproducibility details are missing or underspecified, such as exact learning rates, resize factors at inference, hardware-independent runtime setup, augmentation choices, and full training schedules beyond epochs and optimizer family.

The deployment and efficiency claims are somewhat weakened by the reported inference speed: despite lower FLOPs than ESDNet-L, Freqformer is slower on 4K images. The paper acknowledges this, but the claim of edge/high-resolution suitability would benefit from memory usage, latency across devices, and tiling behavior.

The low-frequency resize ablation reports very high numbers for the low branch alone, but this does not directly translate to final-image quality and may be difficult to interpret against the full model results. The paper could better explain what target/component is being evaluated in those tables.

The evaluation remains mostly within established paired benchmarks. More evidence on real-world out-of-distribution captures, screen/camera variation, failure cases, and color fidelity beyond PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS would strengthen the practical impact claim.
The paper lacks a meaningful limitations or societal-impact discussion, and it does not analyze cases where frequency separation might remove fine legitimate textures or introduce color shifts.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant low-level vision problem, RGB image demoiréing, and evaluates on several standard datasets including TIP2018, LCDMoire, FHDMi, and UHDM.

The proposed dual-branch design is motivated by a plausible decomposition of moiré artifacts into high-frequency texture corruption and low-frequency color distortion, and the crop/resize training strategy is sensible for high-resolution inputs.
Reported quantitative results are competitive, with consistent gains over many demoiréing baselines and a reasonably compact parameter count compared with several prior models.
The paper includes multiple ablations covering the decomposition choice, low-branch resize strategy, learnable FCT, and architectural components.
weaknesses: The claimed novelty is substantially overstated. The frequency decomposition is essentially a fixed smoothing/residual split inspired by prior work, while the architecture combines familiar ingredients: encoder-decoder restoration, channel attention, depthwise projections, RDDB-style local blocks, and feature fusion. The paper does not make a strong case that these pieces amount to a conceptually new contribution.

The experimental evidence does not convincingly isolate the proposed ideas. Several ablations change parameter counts, branch structures, or training/inference protocols at the same time, making it hard to attribute gains specifically to the decomposition, FCT, SA-CA, or resize strategy.

The comparison protocol is under-specified. It is unclear which baselines are reproduced, retrained, taken from papers, or adapted, and whether all methods receive comparable training schedules, input resolutions, data augmentation, and inference strategies. This is especially important because many reported gains are modest.

The method is presented as efficient and suitable for high-resolution or edge deployment, but the paper reports slower 4K inference than ESDNet-L despite lower FLOPs, and gives no memory footprint, latency across devices, or deployment evidence. The edge-device claim is therefore unsupported.

Reproducibility is weak: the abstract says code will be released but no usable link is provided, and important implementation details such as decomposition level, padding/boundary handling, exact resize scales, loss-layer choices, and baseline adaptation details are insufficiently specified.

The motivation for low-frequency color correction partly relies on dataset-induced color shifts, but the paper does not analyze whether the method corrects real moiré artifacts versus benchmark alignment/color biases. Cross-dataset or real-world generalization experiments would be important.

The writing and presentation are uneven, with grammatical issues, vague claims such as “awesome benefits,” broken equation rendering, and several assertions about DWT/DCT limitations that are not rigorously justified. This hurts clarity and scientific confidence.
Overall, while the empirical tables show promise, the contribution appears incremental and the evidence is not strong enough to support the breadth of the claims for an ECCV acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical low-level vision problem, image demoiréing, with a well-motivated decomposition of moiré artifacts into high-frequency texture corruption and low-frequency color distortion. The resulting dual-branch design is intuitive and well aligned with the observed artifact structure.

Experimental results are strong across several standard demoiréing benchmarks, including TIP2018, LCDMoire, FHDMi, and UHDM. The method is consistently competitive or state of the art on PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS, while using a relatively compact 6.1M-parameter model.

The paper provides useful ablations for the main design choices: the proposed frequency decomposition versus Haar/DCT alternatives, resize-based low-frequency training, learnable FCT, hierarchical fusion, RDDB, SCP, and SA-CA variants. These ablations make the empirical case substantially more convincing.

The method is practically attractive for high-resolution demoiréing: it explicitly considers 4K inputs, reports FLOPs and inference time, and compares against both specialized demoiréing methods and recent general restoration models.

The presentation is generally clear, with visualizations that help explain why high- and low-frequency components should be handled differently. The qualitative examples support the quantitative trends, especially for residual moiré and color correction.
weaknesses: The originality is solid but not decisive. The frequency decomposition is essentially a smooth low-pass/high-pass recursive filtering scheme inspired by prior work, and the FCT fusion is relatively simple. The paper would benefit from a sharper explanation of what is fundamentally new beyond adapting known frequency decomposition, dual-branch restoration, and channel-attention ideas to demoiréing.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence fully supports. For example, the discussion of DWT/DCT limitations and error accumulation is plausible, but mostly argued qualitatively; the empirical comparison is useful, yet the variants also have different parameter counts and architectural adaptations, making it hard to isolate the transform alone.

The deployment/edge-device motivation is only partially supported. Although the parameter count and FLOPs are favorable, the reported 4K inference speed is slower than ESDNet-L, and memory usage is not reported. This weakens the practical efficiency claim.

Reproducibility details are incomplete in places. The abstract says code will be released but the URL is absent, and some training details for adapted baselines, runtime measurement conditions, and exact resizing/cropping/inference settings are not fully specified.

The evaluation is broad on established paired benchmarks, but there is limited analysis of robustness to real-world distribution shifts, different capture devices, screen types, or failure cases. Since demoiréing is highly device- and scene-dependent, this leaves some uncertainty about generalization.

The paper does not include a meaningful limitations or societal-impact discussion. This is not fatal for this technical contribution, but acknowledging failure modes such as over-smoothing fine screen/text details, color shifts from misaligned pairs, or device-specific behavior would improve the scientific framing.
